chapter: Split, hospital and decline of tap
title: Chuck and Chuckles continued with Harold Kroma
summary: Green performs a year and a half as Chuck and Chuckles with Harold Kroma playing Chuckles, working the Roxy and Loew's, but it was not the same without Chuckles' scat.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: And what were you doing in the interim -- those two years while he was married?
Well, I improved myself, you see. I

improved myself, I got -- I was allowed to instruct another person to play my role as Chuck, you know, and I did what I could of Chuckles. I played the part of Chuckles. So, the other person and I, we did Chuck and Chuckles for about a year and a half.
Who was this other person?
It was Gloria Kroma's husband, Harold Kroma.
This was Harold?

Yes, yes. He was known as the Monitor, you know, the Jazz Monitor, see, at that time. Sammy Davis, Jr., -- he was inspired by Harold Kroma, the Jazz Monitor. As you know, Sammy Davis, Jr., reached all heights, you know.
(Recording interruption)
So, Harold and you teamed up to become the new Chuck and Chuckles.
Right, yes, George.
And that lasted for how long?

One year and a half because I had to be ready to go back in -- that's what I really thought. I thought that after the two years was up again that Chuckles and I would reunion sure enough. We couldn't neglect the public anymore, because they wanted to see the real, you know, see. Because the way he played the vibraphone and done that operatic scattin' -- scattin', see, singin', see. See, the Jazz Monitor couldn't get up that far, you see. So, Chuckles agreed, you know, that

that would -- we would do this, see. Now, I got involved with a voucher. I can't let the voucher -- I can't disappoint the voucher, so I figured, I said, "Well, I'll go out up there in Long Island -- West Brentwood, Long Island, and get in the tournaments, you know, go to the doctors, you see, and let them reinstate my physical well-being, what I call it, (unintelligible)
In other words, you were feeling lousy.
Huh?
You were feeling very bad. You had left -- Chuckles wasn't willing to go back into the group and you had split up from Kroma, so you decided to go to a hospital at that time.

Yes, well, that's as far as we agreed to go anyhow. I mean, we wasn't -- see, we were -- our business was introduced by an office, you see, like say Nat Nazzaro. He didn't want me to be depressed and he thought maybe I'd go and turn into a gambler or something, you see, and then -- I did not. I didn't want to violate any, you know -- couldn't afford to have any bad rumors, you know, like have any bad habits of being -- you know, panhandler or anything like that, you know, a peddler, you know. You couldn't do this.
And you weren't working then, either?
Well, I weren't working -- I worked for that year and a half with the Jazz Monitor as Chuck and Chuckles.

That's Harold Kroma --you know. We worked quite a ways there. We went -- where did we go? Yeah, we worked the Roxy -- that wasn't bad. We worked the Proctor's, that's here in New York City. That's Loew's Circuit, the Loew's Circuit we worked.
What was the audience response to the new Chuck?

Stopped the show, you know -- stopped the show. But it was not the same -- couldn't be, you know, because like I say, he's known as Jimmy "Chuckles" Walker after that, you know. He used to do that operatic scatting, you know -- scat singing, you know. It was -- naturally the Jazz Monitor couldn't do that. I mean, they all wanted to do it, but Chuckles was the only one -- he was one of a kind with that kind of singing, you see. Because he -- yeah, I mean, I'm still laughing, you know.
